spec.title: Ingest request time p50 and p99 (k6)
spec.description: What the client sees. The hypothesis says this stays flat while Postgres is slow, because the API only writes to Kafka. A rise that starts when the toxic goes on (see the run phase panel) would mean the API depends on the database after all, which would be surprising. k6 series are not marked stale after a run, so the last value can linger for minutes.

spec.title: Offered, accepted and stored events per second
spec.description: Accepted (202) per second should stay at the offered rate all run. Rows inserted per second is what the sink gets into Postgres: expect it to fall below the accepted line while the database is slow and to jump above it after recovery while the lag is drained. The area between the two lines is the lag.

spec.title: Consumer lag (records not yet in Postgres)
spec.description: Total over all partitions, from the sink's own lag gauge (log end offset minus committed offset, polled every second). Flat near zero while healthy; a straight line up while the sink is slower than the arrivals; a line down after recovery. A curve that levels off while the toxic is still on means the sink adapted (bigger chunks) and is no longer slower than the arrivals.

spec.title: Run phase and injected latency
spec.description: Phase: 0 healthy, 1 slow, 2 after (toxic removed, load still on), 3 load finished and draining, -1 no run. Slow ms is the latency the toxic adds to every Postgres answer right now. Added by this experiment (run.sh writes it to a textfile), so it only exists after the first run.

spec.title: Lag per partition
spec.description: The key is the same for every partition, so the six lines should grow together. One line growing faster would mean uneven load, not the slow database.

spec.title: Postgres write time seen by the sink (avg and p99)
spec.description: One write transaction = BEGIN, INSERT, COMMIT. With the toxic every answer is delayed, so the time should rise by about three times the added latency. If it rises by much less, the sink is not going through the proxy and the whole run is invalid.

spec.title: Rows per chunk (average)
spec.description: The sink writes one chunk per transaction, at most 1000 rows. When writes get slower, more records are waiting and the chunks get bigger, which raises the sink's capacity. A line that climbs to 1000 and stays there means the sink is at its chunk limit; that limit decides whether lag grows without end.

spec.title: Chunk processing time p99 (parse + write + commit)
spec.description: The whole chunk including the offset commit to Kafka (not slowed). Mostly the write time, plus a little.

spec.title: Freshness p99 (API receive to row committed)
spec.description: How old an event is when it becomes visible in Postgres. It should follow the lag: lag divided by the sink rate. Top histogram bucket may clamp the value; check the bucket limits in sink-stats.ts.

spec.title: Kafka end offset and committed offset (all partitions)
spec.description: Records written to the topic against records the group has committed. The gap is the lag, seen from Kafka's side (kafka_exporter, scraped every few seconds, so it is coarser than the sink gauge).

spec.title: Topic size on the brokers' disks
spec.description: Bytes of the k7-events partition directories in each broker's log dir, replicas included (3 copies in total). Added by this experiment (infra/scripts/kafka-disk-exporter.sh, sampled every 2 s). It grows with what the API writes, whether or not the consumer keeps up: that is the point, a slow consumer does not make the log larger, only retention decides when it is deleted. Retention is 1 day here, so nothing is deleted during a run.

spec.title: Log written per second and unread backlog in bytes (estimate)
spec.description: Disk growth of all three brokers together, as a rate. If the unread backlog in bytes (lag x average bytes per record) approaches the retention limit the consumer would lose data; here retention is far away, so this is only the size of what is waiting. The average bytes per record is topic bytes / topic end offset, so it includes the 3 replicas: divide by 3 for one copy.

spec.title: Consumer process CPU (cores)
spec.description: The slow database makes the sink wait, not compute: CPU should drop during the slow window and rise again when it catches up with a big backlog. A pinned-at-1-core line would mean the sink is CPU bound, which changes the recovery prediction.

spec.title: Host CPU busy of the pinned groups
spec.description: Busy share of the CPUs each group is pinned to (server, consumer, brokers, k6, monitoring + Postgres + Toxiproxy). Keep the k6 group under about 70% so the generator is not the limit.

spec.title: Postgres connections waiting in the sink's pool
spec.description: The sink writes one chunk at a time, so this should stay 0 even when slow. A value above 0 would mean several writers fight for the pool.

spec.title: k6 dropped iterations
spec.description: Must be 0 in a measured run. Anything else means k6 could not keep the rate.

spec.title: k6 failed requests
spec.description: Share of requests that did not get a successful answer. Must be 0: the API does not use Postgres.

spec.title: API acknowledged messages per second
spec.description: Records Kafka acknowledged to the API (acks=all). Should equal the offered rate in every window.

spec.title: API 503s and Kafka send errors
spec.description: Must stay 0. A rise means the API shed load, which is not what this experiment is about.

spec.title: Chunk failures, retries and DLQ
spec.description: A slow database should not fail chunks: they just take longer. Failures or retries mean a timeout was hit (a second source of lag that is not plain slowness). The DLQ must stay 0.

spec.title: Rebalances of the consumer group
spec.description: One at the start of each run is normal. A rise during the slow window would mean the consumer was kicked out of the group (a poll or heartbeat timeout), and the lag would then include a pause, not only slowness.

spec.title: Event loop lag p99 (API and sink)
spec.description: Node's event loop delay. High values on the API would make its latency number meaningless; on the sink they would add to the processing time.

spec.title: 1. The verdict: does ingestion notice the slow database?
2. The mechanism: why lag grows and how fast it comes back
3. Resource view: where the cost lands
4. Validity checks: can I trust this run
